description: The principles underpinning law: presumption of innocence and equality before the law.
content_html:
What Would Society Look Like Without Laws?

Imagine a world with no rules about property, violence, or fairness. Without a system to settle disputes and protect people from harm, individuals would rely entirely on their own strength or the strength of those around them. Laws exist to prevent exactly this. Laws are formal rules backed by the power of the state. They apply to everyone and provide a system for resolving disputes, protecting rights, and expressing society’s shared values.

Rules and laws help society address complex problems of fairness, justice and discrimination. A law against workplace discrimination, for example, does not just protect one individual — it shapes how employers across the whole country behave. The same is true of laws around education, housing, health and safety, and the environment. Laws give individuals enforceable rights and hold both people and institutions to account.

Key Fact

Two fundamental principles underpin the UK legal system. First, the presumption of innocence: every person accused of a crime is considered innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt. Second, equality before the law: the law applies to everyone in the same way, regardless of wealth, status or background.

The Presumption of Innocence

The presumption of innocence is one of the most important protections in a fair legal system. It means the burden of proof lies with the prosecution, not the defendant. In a criminal trial in England and Wales, the prosecution must prove that the accused committed the offence “beyond reasonable doubt” — a high standard designed to prevent wrongful convictions.

This principle protects individuals from the power of the state. Without it, governments or powerful interests could imprison people simply by making an accusation. The presumption of innocence is recognised in Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights, which guarantees the right to a fair trial, and in the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights (Article 11). It is also central to the common law tradition that England has developed over centuries.

Different legal proceedings use different standards of proof. In criminal cases, the prosecution must prove guilt beyond reasonable doubt — this high bar protects defendants from wrongful conviction, since a criminal conviction can mean a prison sentence. In civil cases — disputes between individuals rather than state prosecutions — the standard is lower: the balance of probabilities, meaning it is more likely than not that the claimant’s account is correct. The difference reflects the much more serious consequences of criminal conviction compared to a civil remedy such as compensation.

Equality Before the Law

Equality before the law means that no person stands above the law. A wealthy business owner charged with fraud faces the same legal process as anyone else. A government minister who breaks the law is subject to the same courts as a private citizen. This principle is part of the broader concept of the rule of law — the idea that government itself is bound by law, not just individuals.

The rule of law is a cornerstone of democratic societies. It means that laws must be publicly known, applied consistently, and enforced by an independent judiciary. When courts are independent from government pressure, individuals can challenge state decisions. In the UK, the Supreme Court has ruled against government actions on several occasions, including in constitutional cases. This judicial independence is considered essential to equality before the law in practice, not just in theory.

Rights do not exist in isolation. In a diverse society, one person’s rights can conflict with another’s. A property owner’s right to quiet enjoyment may conflict with a neighbour’s right to hold a political demonstration outside. Freedom of expression can conflict with a person’s right to privacy or protection from harassment. The law attempts to balance competing rights through legislation, court judgements and international agreements.

The European Convention on Human Rights includes both absolute rights (which cannot be limited under any circumstances, such as the prohibition on torture) and qualified rights (which can be limited in specific circumstances to protect the rights of others or the wider public interest, such as freedom of movement or freedom of expression). Understanding where rights can be balanced against responsibilities is central to citizenship and to how courts make decisions in complex cases.

Why Society Needs Laws: a Broader Picture

Laws serve several interconnected functions in modern society. They protect individuals from harm by others. They define the boundaries of acceptable behaviour in public and in private. They provide a mechanism for resolving disputes peacefully without resort to violence. They express the values that society has decided to uphold, such as prohibiting discrimination on grounds of race, gender or disability. And they enable complex economic and social activities — contracts, property rights, corporate structures — that would be impossible without a reliable legal framework that all parties can trust.

Key Fact

Key pieces of legislation that have extended legal rights in the UK include the Representation of the People Act (which progressively widened voting rights), the Equal Pay Act 1970 (equal pay for men and women), the Race Relations Act 1976 (which outlawed racial discrimination in employment and housing), and the Human Rights Act 1998 (which incorporated European Convention rights into domestic law).

Rights and responsibilities exist in local, national and global contexts. At a local level, planning laws govern what you can build on your property and protect your neighbours. At a national level, criminal and civil law set the framework for how disputes are resolved. At a global level, international agreements such as the UN Universal Declaration of Human Rights and the Geneva Conventions establish standards that countries are expected to meet. In all three contexts, rights and responsibilities must be balanced: a right to free speech, for example, comes with the responsibility not to use that speech to incite violence or hatred.
exam_tip_html: For ‘Discuss’ and ‘Evaluate’ questions about law and rights, always distinguish between principles (the presumption of innocence, equality before the law, the rule of law) and how they work in practice. Top-band answers name a real piece of legislation or a real institution to show the principle in action — for example, the Human Rights Act 1998 as the way ECHR rights are enforced domestically, or the Supreme Court’s independence as how equality before the law is protected. For a ‘Discuss’ question asking whether the law always achieves fairness, you must present at least two viewpoints: one that supports the statement (examples of the law protecting individuals) and one that challenges it (examples where access to justice is unequal, such as the cost of legal representation). Use connectives like ‘however’ and ‘on the other hand’ to signal that you are weighing viewpoints, not just listing them. Avoid summarising the question back to the examiner — make a point, develop it, and link it back to the question.
conclusion_html:
Key Takeaways

  • Laws exist to protect rights, resolve disputes, express shared values and enable social and economic life — without them, individuals would have no reliable protection against the power of others or the state.
  • The presumption of innocence means a defendant is considered innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt; equality before the law means the same rules apply to everyone regardless of status or wealth.
  • Rights and responsibilities must be balanced at local, national and global levels — key legislation such as the Equal Pay Act 1970 and the Human Rights Act 1998 shows how the UK has progressively extended and protected citizens’ rights through law.

practice_questions.text:
Which of the following best describes the presumption of innocence?
A) The accused must prove they did not commit the crime
B) The judge decides whether someone is guilty before the trial begins
C) A person is considered innocent until the prosecution proves guilt
D) A person found guilty once is always treated as likely to reoffend
practice_questions.marks: 1 mark for C) A person is considered innocent until the prosecution proves guilt.

practice_questions.text: State what is meant by the rule of law.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 2 marks:
1 mark for a basic statement (e.g. everyone must obey the law / the law applies to everyone including the government).
2 marks for a more precise statement that includes the idea that government itself is bound by law and that an independent judiciary enforces it, or that laws must be publicly known and applied consistently.

Credit equivalent accurate answers. Do not credit vague answers such as 'following the rules' without any further development.

practice_questions.text: Explain why the presumption of innocence is considered an essential principle of a fair legal system.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks. A single fully developed point with cause and consequence can score up to 3 marks; two developed points can score 4. Credit the following or equivalent reasoning:

1 mark for identifying the principle (accused is innocent until proven guilty beyond reasonable doubt).
1 mark for explaining why this matters (places burden of proof on the prosecution, not the defendant).
1 mark for a developed consequence (without it, the state could imprison people simply by making an accusation / protects individuals from state power).
1 mark for linking to a named source or real-world application (Article 6 ECHR / the right to a fair trial / UK criminal court procedure).

Do not credit answers that describe only what the principle is without explaining why it is necessary.

practice_questions.text:
Read the extract below and answer the question that follows.

A fictional article in a national newspaper states: 'A 2024 survey of 2,000 adults by a civic research organisation found that 34% of respondents from lower-income households said they could not afford legal representation if they faced a civil dispute, compared with just 9% of respondents from higher-income households. The survey also found that 68% of all respondents agreed with the statement: "The law treats wealthy and less wealthy people differently in practice."'

What does the source suggest about equality before the law in the UK? Use the source and your own knowledge to support your answer.
practice_questions.marks:
Up to 4 marks:
1 mark for identifying the source's key finding (large gap in ability to afford legal representation between income groups; majority believe the law treats people differently based on wealth).
1 mark for interpreting its significance (suggests formal equality before the law does not always translate into practical equality of access to justice).
1 mark for using own knowledge (e.g. Legal Aid reforms, cost of barristers, the difference between formal legal equality and practical access to justice).
1 mark for a substantiated judgement combining source and knowledge (e.g. the source supports the view that while equality before the law is a formal principle, structural inequalities in access to legal representation mean it is not always achieved in practice).

Do not credit answers that only summarise the survey without interpreting it or connecting it to own knowledge.

practice_questions.text:
"The law always treats people equally, regardless of their background."

Discuss this statement. In your answer, present viewpoints that support it and viewpoints that challenge it.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (7–8 marks): Sustained discussion presenting both viewpoints with named examples on each side. Uses connective language to signal contrast (however, on the other hand, in contrast). Reaches a weighing judgement. Names at least one real-world example per side (e.g. specific legislation or a named institution).

Secure (5–6 marks): Both viewpoints present and developed. At least one named real-world example lifts the answer. Some weighing but judgement may be limited.

Developing (3–4 marks): Relevant points on both sides but limited development OR one-sided. May describe rather than discuss.

Emerging (1–2 marks): Basic relevant points; little real-world reference; descriptive.

Viewpoints supporting the statement: the principle of equality before the law is enshrined in the UK legal system and is protected by an independent judiciary; legislation such as the Equality Act 2010 prohibits discrimination; the Human Rights Act 1998 gives all citizens the right to a fair trial; courts have ruled against powerful public figures and government departments.

Viewpoints challenging the statement: access to high-quality legal representation depends on ability to pay; cuts to Legal Aid have reduced support for those who cannot afford private solicitors; research suggests that members of some ethnic groups are over-represented in the criminal justice system; informal barriers (language, literacy, awareness of rights) mean formal equality does not always translate into equal outcomes in practice.

practice_questions.text:
"The most important reason for having laws is to protect the rights of individuals."

Evaluate this statement. In your answer you should consider arguments that support this view, arguments that challenge it, and reach a substantiated conclusion.
practice_questions.marks:
Mastering (10–12 marks): Full two-sided argument with named examples on each side. Directly engages with the word 'most important' by comparing reasons for having laws. Reaches a substantiated conclusion that goes beyond restating points.

Secure (7–9 marks): Both sides developed with at least one named real-world example. Concludes, but the judgement may be partially substantiated.

Developing (4–6 marks): Relevant arguments on both sides but limited development OR one-sided. Some real-world reference.

Emerging (1–3 marks): Basic points; little real-world example; largely descriptive.

Arguments supporting the statement: Laws such as the Human Rights Act 1998, the Equal Pay Act 1970 and the Race Relations Act 1976 directly protect individual rights; the presumption of innocence protects individuals from state abuse; equal pay law has improved workplace fairness for millions.

Arguments challenging the statement: Laws also serve to maintain public order (criminal law), facilitate economic activity (contract law, property law), express collective social values (environmental law, planning law), and protect society as a whole rather than just individuals. Some would argue that maintaining social order is at least as important as individual rights protection, since without order individual rights cannot be exercised. Others argue that international obligations — such as the Geneva Conventions governing warfare — go beyond individual rights protection entirely.

Conclusion to credit: a judgement that identifies which reason the student finds most compelling and why, with reference to at least one named piece of legislation or institution.

knowledge_checks.q: What does the presumption of innocence mean in a criminal trial?
options: The defendant must prove they are innocent
The judge decides guilt before evidence is heard
The accused is considered innocent until the prosecution proves guilt
Both sides must present equal evidence

knowledge_checks.q: What standard of proof is required in criminal cases in England and Wales?
Equality before the law means that the same rules apply to _____, regardless of wealth or social status.
The _____ Act 1998 incorporated the rights in the European Convention on Human Rights into UK domestic law.
Match each legal principle to its meaning:
right: Accused is considered innocent until guilt is proven by the prosecution
Everyone, including the government, must obey the law
The same legal rules apply to all people regardless of background

flashcard_questions.q: What is the presumption of innocence?
flashcard_questions.a: An accused person is considered innocent until the prosecution proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt.

flashcard_questions.q: What standard of proof must the prosecution meet in a criminal case?
What standard of proof applies in civil cases?
flashcard_questions.a: Balance of probabilities — more likely than not that the claim is true.

flashcard_questions.q: What does equality before the law mean?
flashcard_questions.a: The same legal rules apply to everyone regardless of wealth, status or background.

flashcard_questions.q: What is the rule of law?
flashcard_questions.a: Everyone, including the government, must obey the law; no one is above it.

flashcard_questions.q: Which Act incorporated ECHR rights into UK domestic law?
What did the Equal Pay Act 1970 do?
flashcard_questions.a: Required men and women to receive equal pay for equal work.

flashcard_questions.q: Name one function laws serve in a modern society.
Where is the presumption of innocence protected in international law?
flashcard_questions.a: Article 6 of the European Convention on Human Rights (right to a fair trial).

flashcard_questions.q: What is the difference between an absolute right and a qualified right under the ECHR?
flashcard_questions.a: Absolute rights cannot be limited at all; qualified rights can be limited to protect others or the public interest.

flashcard_questions.q: Give one example of a qualified right under the ECHR.
flashcard_questions.a: Freedom of expression — can be limited to prevent incitement to hatred.

glossary_terms.definition: Formal rules made by a recognised authority and enforced by the state, setting out what people may and may not do and providing consequences for those who break them.
The legal principle that a person accused of a crime is assumed to be innocent until the prosecution proves guilt beyond reasonable doubt.
The standard of proof required in criminal cases, meaning the evidence must be so strong that there is no reasonable alternative explanation.
The standard of proof in civil law cases, meaning it must be more likely than not (over 50% probability) that the claim is true.
The principle that the law applies equally to all people regardless of wealth, social status, ethnicity, gender or political position.
The principle that everyone, including the government and its officials, must obey the law, and that no one is above it.

items.title: In Our Time — The Code of Hammurabi
items.description: Misha Glenny and historians discuss the world's oldest written law code, from 1750 BC Babylon — puts the question 'why do societies need laws?' into fascinating historical perspective.

items.title: In Our Time — On Liberty
items.description: Mill's argument for what the law should and shouldn't do — explores the tension between individual freedom and social order that is central to this lesson.

items.title: You Would Be a Terrible Leader — CGP Grey
items.description: Explains why unchecked personal power leads to poor outcomes for society — makes the case for rule of law and equality before the law from first principles.

items.title: Why The War on Drugs Is a Huge Failure — Kurzgesagt
items.description: Examines what happens when laws fail to achieve their stated purpose — a case study in the relationship between law, public health and equality, stimulating debate about what laws are for.

items.title: Just Mercy (2019)
items.description: The true story of lawyer Bryan Stevenson's fight to free a wrongly convicted man on death row in the US — a powerful case study in the gap between the principle of equality before the law and its practice.

items.title: Selma (2014)
items.description: The story of the 1965 Selma to Montgomery marches for voting rights — shows how civic campaigning can change the law when equality before the law is not delivered in practice.

items.title: Amnesty International UK — Education Resources
items.description: Free resources on human rights law and the rule of law — supports understanding of why laws protecting rights are essential in a democratic society.

items.title: AQA GCSE Citizenship Studies — Specification
items.description: The official AQA specification — check what is examined on legal principles including the presumption of innocence and equality before the law.
